sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: To investigate long-term outcomes for triple‑negative breast cancer (TNBC) patients enrolled in JBCRG-22.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: TNBC (cT1c–T3, cN0–1, M0) patients were stratified by homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) and germline BRCA mutation (gBRCAm) status. Group A patients (aged < 65 years with HRD-positive tumors, or those with gBRCAm, if available) were randomized to receive 4 cycles of weekly paclitaxel (group A1) or eribulin (group A2), both with carboplatin, followed by 4 cycles of anthracycline. Group B patients (aged < 65 years with HRD-negative tumors or aged ≥ 65 years) were randomized to receive 6 cycles of eribulin plus cyclophosphamide (group B1) or eribulin plus capecitabine (group B2). Five-year invasive disease-free survival (IDFS), distant disease-free survival (DDFS), and overall survival (OS) were assessed. Additionally, data were analyzed by biomarker levels including lymphocyte count (LC) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Ninety-nine patients were followed for a median of 5.6 years. In patients who received eribulin-based therapy (groups A2 + B1 + B2), 5-year IDFS and OS rates, respectively, were 95% and 100% in patients who achieved pCR after neoadjuvant therapy (n = 20) and 71.4% and 80.2% in those who did not (n = 56), showing significantly better prognosis in the pCR cohort (p < 0.05). OS tended to be better in patients with baseline LC ≥ 1500/mm3 and NLR < 3, particularly in eribulin-treated patients, although differences were non-significant.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings will help guide the development of eribulin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy for selected TNBC patients. Our exploratory analysis of LC and NLR results may help inform clinical prediction models for eribulin-treated patients.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: The study has been registered with the University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry (https://www.umin.ac.jp/ctr/index-j.htm) with unique trial number UMIN000023162. The Japan Breast Cancer Research Group trial number is JBCRG-22.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is challenging to treat owing to a lack of specific targets, and it has a poor prognosis compared with hormone receptor-positive or human epidermal growth factor 2-positive breast cancer [1, 2]. Perioperative chemotherapy with anthracycline- and taxane-based regimens has been the mainstay of systemic therapy for TNBC; however, response and survival rates remain low, necessitating alternative treatment strategies [3]. Previous studies have shown the benefit, in terms of pathological complete response (pCR) rate, of adding carboplatin to anthracycline-plus-taxane-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy for TNBC patients [4, 5], based on the observation that carboplatin has pronounced benefits in patients with germline BRCA mutation (gBRCAm) [6]. The phase III KEYNOTE-522 trial showed a significantly increased pCR rate when the programmed death (PD)−1 inhibitor pembrolizumab was added to neoadjuvant paclitaxel and carboplatin for treatment-naïve patients with early-stage TNBC [7], thus establishing this combination as one of the standard regimens for this population.

In search of novel therapeutic strategies, we conducted the Japan Breast Cancer Research Group 22 (JBCRG-22) study to investigate the clinical usefulness of eribulin-containing neoadjuvant regimens for TNBC [8]. Our rationale for this approach is based on eribulin’s unique mechanisms of action as a first-in-class microtubule inhibitor that disrupts mitosis, promotes vascular remodeling, and suppresses epithelial–mesenchymal transition [9–13], thereby enhancing the tumor immune microenvironment. Eribulin has been shown to be effective in the treatment of advanced or recurrent breast cancer, including TNBC [14, 15], with one pooled analysis showing particular benefit for patients with TNBC [15]. Its potential benefit when added to neoadjuvant chemotherapy for TNBC has also been reported previously [16, 17].

In the JBCRG-22 study, patients were prospectively stratified based on homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) score [18] and available data regarding gBRCAm status [6], which are established predictors of pCR, in order to identify those who may benefit most from the study regimens. We found that, in patients aged < 65 years with high HRD score (HRD-positive tumors) or with gBRCAm (if available), weekly paclitaxel-plus-carboplatin and eribulin-plus-carboplatin regimens, each followed by anthracycline, resulted in high pCR rate (> 60% and > 40%, respectively). Notably, neurotoxicity, a common adverse event (AE) of chemotherapy, was less frequent in patients treated with the eribulin-based regimens. This finding raised the possibility that eribulin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be worth exploring as a treatment option for TNBC patients, for whom AEs are likely to have a greater negative impact [8].

Here, we describe a follow-up study of JBCRG-22 in which we investigated the long-term outcomes for patients who received eribulin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy compared with those who received a standard paclitaxel-based regimen, with the results stratified by pCR status. A post hoc analysis of data from the landmark phase III EMBRACE study [19] showed high absolute lymphocyte count (LC) (≥ 1500/µL) to be significantly associated with longer overall survival (OS) in patients with metastatic breast cancer treated with eribulin, but not in those who received treatment based on the physician’s choice. Several other studies have also shown that LC, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and/or platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) may serve as predictive markers of treatment efficacy and prognosis in patients receiving eribulin for advanced or recurrent breast cancer [20–22]. These findings raise the question of whether similar associations can be observed and validated in patients with primary breast cancer. Therefore, in the present study, we also explored relations between baseline LC, NLR, and PLR and pCR or survival outcomes in the patients who participated in the JBCRG-22 study.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: The JBCRG-22 study was a multicenter randomized parallel-group phase II clinical trial for which patients were enrolled in Japan between February 2017 and January 2019. The details of inclusion and exclusion criteria have been reported previously [8]. Briefly, patients were eligible if they had been diagnosed with primary TNBC (resectable tumor; cT1c–cT3, cN0–cN1, and cM0), confirmed as invasive by centralized pathologic review (CPR), had a tumor diameter ≤ 70 mm, and had a Ki67 labeling index ≥ 10% (based on available data). Patients who met the primary registration criteria were evaluated by CPR at Kyoto University Hospital (Kyoto, Japan) and were enrolled if they satisfied the secondary registration criteria described previously [8].

Patients were stratified by HRD score, gBRCAm status (based on available data), and age at time of informed consent, and allocated to group A, which included those aged < 65 years and with HRD score ≥ 42 (HRD-positive tumors), and all patients with a record of gBRCAm, or group B, which included those aged < 65 years and with HRD score < 42 (HRD-negative tumors), and all patients aged ≥ 65 years except those with a record of gBRCAm.

Patients in group A were randomized to either group A1, receiving 4 cycles of weekly paclitaxel (80 mg/m2 on days 1, 8, and 15 of each cycle), or group A2, receiving eribulin (1.4 mg/m2) on days 1 and 8 of each cycle, both with carboplatin (AUC6 on day 1). Depending on the antitumor response evaluated after cycle 4 of the initial therapy, patients received an anthracycline-based regimen before surgery or discontinued chemotherapy and underwent surgery. The anthracycline-based regimen comprised FEC, consisting of 5-fluorouracil (500 mg/m2), epirubicin (100 mg/m2), and cyclophosphamide (500 mg/m2), or AC, consisting of doxorubicin (60 mg/m2) and cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2), on day 1 of each cycle. Patients in group B were randomized to either group B1, receiving 4 cycles of eribulin (1.4 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 of each cycle) plus cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2 on day 1), or group B2, receiving 4 cycles of eribulin (1.4 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 of each cycle) plus capecitabine (2000 mg/m2/day administered orally twice daily on days 1–14). Depending on the antitumor effects, assessed after cycle 4 of the initial therapy, patients continued to receive an additional two cycles of the eribulin-based regimen, or were switched to the rescue regimen (FEC or AC, as described for group A) before surgery (Supplementary Fig. 1).
The study was registered at the University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry (https://www.umin.ac.jp/ctr/index-j.htm) with the identifier UMIN000023162.

sec.title: Observation and endpoints
sec.p: The following items were evaluated at 6 months and at 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 years after secondary registration (± 2 months): metastasis or recurrence, development of secondary cancer, survival, postoperative treatment details, and outcome of grade ≥ 2 AEs that occurred during the study and for which a causal relationship with the clinical trial cannot be ruled out.

In the present follow-up analysis, endpoints included 5-year invasive disease-free survival (IDFS), distant disease-free survival (DDFS), and OS. IDFS was defined as the time from the date of secondary registration to the date of onset of one of the following: confirmation of cancer involving the ipsilateral breast; recurrence in lymph nodes in the ipsilateral axillary region, chest wall, or skin; confirmation of metastasis to distant organs; death from any cause; confirmation of invasive breast cancer on the opposite side; and confirmation of primary invasive cancer in other organs. Distant disease-free survival (DDFS) was defined as the time from the date of secondary registration to death from any cause, distant recurrence of breast cancer, or the event of a secondary cancer (date of onset of the event), whichever occurred first. OS was defined as the time from the date of secondary registration to death from any cause. Patients who were alive during the present analysis period were censored on the date of the last confirmation of survival. Additionally, for exploratory purposes, survival data were analyzed by the levels of peripheral blood markers (LC, NLR, and PLR) at baseline. Pathological complete response was defined as CpCRypN0.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: For the analyses of IDFS, DDFS, and OS, the Kaplan–Meier method was used to estimate survival curves, and the log-rank test was used for comparisons between the groups. To analyze the treatment effects, hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each group, using the Cox proportional hazards model.
The level of statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Statistical analyses were carried out using R (version 4.5.0; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

sec.title: Ethical considerations
sec.p: The study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant ethical guidelines for clinical studies. It was approved by the ethics committee at each institution at the start of the study, and additional approval was obtained for the present follow-up study. All patients provided informed consent at the start of the study. Additional consent was considered unnecessary because the follow-up did not involve any interventions; all data were collected from the patients’ medical records.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: For the present follow-up study, the data cut-off date was March 31, 2024. All 99 patients enrolled in the JBCRG-22 study (23 and 22 in groups A1 and A2, respectively, and 27 each in groups B1 and B2, respectively) were included in the present analysis and were followed up for a median of 5.6 years.

Table 1 summarizes the patients’ characteristics at baseline. The characteristics of groups A and B were generally well balanced. Median tumor size was 27.0 mm (range, 12–92 mm), and 63% of patients had cN0 tumors. There were no cases of invasive lobular carcinoma. sec.title: Survival outcomes
sec.p:
Table 2 summarizes responses to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and 5-year survival rates in each treatment group. Patients in groups A1 and A2, who had pCR rates after neoadjuvant chemotherapy of 65% (15/23) and 45% (10/22), respectively, had favorable survival outcomes, with 5-year DDFS and OS exceeding 90%. In contrast, patients in groups B1 and B2, who had a pCR rate of 19% (5/27), had lower 5-year survival rates (IDFS and DDFS, 70%–78%; OS, 81%–86%); notably, however, the 5-year OS rate for patients in group B who achieved pCR was 100% (10/10). Relations between levels of pretreatment peripheral markers (LC, NLR, and PLR) and treatment efficacy (i.e., pCR after neoadjuvant therapy), investigated for exploratory, hypothesis-generating purposes, are summarized in the Supplementary Table. No significant associations were identified.

Other results from the exploratory analysis of peripheral marker data are shown in Fig. 3. This shows OS according to LC (Fig. 3A) and NLR (Fig. 3B) in patients who received standard therapy (i.e., group A1) and a combined group of patients who received eribulin-based therapy (i.e., groups A2 + B1 + B2). OS tended to be better in patients with LC ≥ 1500/mm3 and NLR < 3, particularly in patients who received eribulin-based therapy, although differences were not significant in any subgroup. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The JBCRG-22 study is, to our knowledge, the first to evaluate neoadjuvant eribulin for TNBC in the prospective randomized setting, based on stratification by HRD score and recorded gBRCAm status. In this long-term follow-up study, patients who achieved pCR after neoadjuvant eribulin-based therapy had a favorable prognosis. Although this association has been previously reported for taxane-based therapy, the present study is the first to show this association with an eribulin-based regimen.

In patients with HRD-positive tumors (group A), 5-year DDFS and OS were > 90% in patients who received eribulin-based therapy, which is a similar value to outcomes observed with the standard paclitaxel-based regimen. Moreover, in group A patients who achieved pCR, the 5-year IDFS and OS rates were 92.0% and 95.7%, respectively, indicating a favorable long-term prognosis.

In the combined group of patients who received eribulin-based therapy (groups A2, B1, and B2), the pCR rate was 26% (20/76). For those who achieved pCR, the 5-year IDFS and OS rates were 95.0% and 100%, respectively. These findings indicate the possibility that if patients with high sensitivity to eribulin can be identified, there may be a role for eribulin-based regimens in the treatment of subgroups within this population. For example, TNBC patients with HRD-positive tumors or at greater risk of developing neuropathy might be expected to benefit from the lower incidence of peripheral neuropathy when an eribulin-based therapy is used instead of taxanes [8]. Evidence from larger scale trials, including comparisons with contemporary standard treatments, would be needed before eribulin-based therapy could be established as a taxane-avoiding treatment for specific groups of eribulin-sensitive patients.

The clinical relevance of HRD-positive and gBRCAm status in the prognostic stratification of breast cancer patients has been supported by previous research. A study using genomic and transcriptomic analyses of tumor samples reported higher pCR rates in patients with BRCA2-mutated tumors (83%) compared to those with non-BRCA2-mutated tumors (36%). The study also suggested that fibroblast growth factor receptor-2 (FGFR2) expression may play a role in the response to eribulin and carboplatin treatment [23]. In a recent study that assessed HRD status in 225 consecutive patients with TNBC, 53.3% were HRD-positive, and the pCR rate was significantly greater in patients with HRD-positive or high HRD score tumors and associated with extended distant metastasis-free survival and OS [24]. These findings are consistent with our results for group A in the present study and further highlight the prognostic value of HRD assessment in TNBC patients receiving neoadjuvant eribulin-based therapy. Based on our data, we suggest that HRD-positive status may be clinically useful for identifying patients who could benefit from eribulin-containing neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

In the present study, for exploratory, hypothesis-generating purposes, we also investigated whether baseline levels of peripheral blood markers (LC, NLR, and PLR) could contribute to the prediction of treatment efficacy and prognosis, based on the findings from the previous studies [19–22]. In our prespecified exploratory analyses stratified by baseline LC, NLR, and PLR, the pCR rate after neoadjuvant therapy did not differ significantly. By contrast, a trend toward improved long-term outcomes (i.e., 5-year DDFS and OS rates) was observed in patients with baseline LC ≥ 1500/mm3 and NLR < 3, particularly in those receiving eribulin-based treatment. Both LC ≥ 1500/mm3 and NLR < 3 reflect the same underlying immune environment. A low NLR suggests that lymphocytes, key players in the specific immune response, are proportionally more abundant than neutrophils, which are typically elevated during inflammation. The findings of the present study suggest that, although these markers may not predict the short-term efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (i.e., achieving pCR), they may be useful in the development of models for the prediction of long-term prognosis, such as recurrence or breast cancer-specific mortality, in eribulin-treated patients, including those who did not achieve pCR. The results are valuable not only in supporting previous findings in advanced or recurrent breast cancer but also in highlighting their relevance to primary TNBC. The lack of significant associations between LC, NLR, and PLR and pCR rate may be because these factors do not reflect the tumor environment; they are non-specific markers of inflammation, whose levels may fluctuate for multiple reasons and throughout the day; their levels in the peripheral blood may not reflect their levels within the tumor itself; and pCR depends on non-immunological as well as immunological factors.

The inferior clinical outcome results (IDFS, DDFS, and OS) for group B patients, namely those with HRD-negative tumors or aged ≥ 65 years, vs group A patients (see Supplementary Fig. 2A–C) suggest the possibility of undertreatment due to not receiving standard taxane-based therapy. Instead of standard therapy, the group B patients were treated using novel eribulin-based regimens that did not include carboplatin, and although rescue treatment with an anthracycline-based regimen was available (based on response to neoadjuvant therapy), this may not have been sufficient to compensate for the potential loss of treatment efficacy. However, about one-fifth of group B patients were able to achieve pCR with the eribulin-based treatment, thus raising the possibility of a benefit through avoidance of taxane- and anthracycline-related toxicities in patients with high sensitivity to eribulin. Additionally, the long-term results presented here show that patients who had achieved pCR with eribulin-based neoadjuvant therapy had a favorable prognosis, similar to that achieved by patients who received conventional taxane- and anthracycline-based regimens.

Regarding clinical implications, this was an exploratory, hypothesis-generating study; therefore, further research is necessary before it becomes possible to confidently position eribulin-based approaches within the current therapeutic landscape. The results of the KEYNOTE-522 trial [7], alongside other trials of PD-1 inhibitors (and PD ligand 1 inhibitors), have contributed to the establishment of current standards for the treatment of patients with high-risk early-stage TNBC, using platinum–taxane with or without immunotherapy; pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy has been approved in the USA for the treatment of such patients in the neoadjuvant setting. Based on the lower-than-expected pCR rate and IDFS, DDFS, and OS in patients in groups B1 and B2 compared with those in groups A1 and A2 in the present study, it is unlikely that eribulin-based regimens would supplant other regimens as current standard therapy for TNBC. However, they may have a role in the treatment of selected patient populations identified as eribulin-sensitive and considered likely to benefit from taxane avoidance.

Further progress in the development of novel eribulin-based regimens will require identification of the patient populations most likely to benefit from their use, for example, through research focusing on new biomarkers predicting the likelihood of achieving pCR. This, in turn, could contribute toward eribulin-based therapy potentially becoming an option for avoiding long-term sequelae of taxane-related peripheral neuropathy or chronic immune-related AEs [25].

Tumors with high HRD might be expected to be especially susceptible to immunotherapy, because they tend to be genomically unstable and often harbor numerous gene mutations and therefore an increased number of neoantigens recognized by immune cells [26]. However, despite HRD contributing to tumor immunogenicity, and often coexisting with immune activation in cases of TNBC, it does not reliably predict responsiveness to immunotherapy in TNBC patients [27]. However, the association between HRD score and sensitivity to anticancer drugs (e.g., platinum-based agents) has been investigated. In one study, BRCA1/2-mutated and HRD-positive patients with TNBC were found to potentially benefit from platinum-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy [28]. In another study, HRD-positive TNBC patients treated with carboplatin had higher pCR rate [24]. A high HRD score is an important factor because genomic instability leads to an increased neoantigen burden, which in turn promotes higher levels of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and ultimately enhances sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors. It therefore holds promise for future treatment individualization based on tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte levels or HRD scores.

Regarding low HRD scores, in patients with HRD-negative tumors (e.g., those in groups B1 and B2 in the present study), eribulin-based or conventional chemotherapy yields insufficient benefit in terms of therapeutic outcomes and prognosis. In such cases, strategies that can induce stronger tumor cell death, such as combining highly immunogenic antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) with immune checkpoint inhibitors, are warranted.

Recently, the results of randomized phase III trials have provided support for the use of ADCs, particularly those targeting the trophoblast cell surface antigen 2, as first-line treatments for patients with advanced TNBC who are not candidates for immunotherapy with PD-1 or PD ligand 1 inhibitors. In the ASCENT-03 trial (n = 558), sacituzumab govitecan-hziy reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 38% (p < 0.0001) when compared against chemotherapy [29]. A similar reduction (43%, p < 0.0001) was achieved, alongside significantly improved OS, in the TROPION-Breast02 trial of datopotamab deruxtecan-dlnk vs chemotherapy (n = 644) [30, 31]. Regarding HER2-targeting ADCs, the results of the phase III DESTINY-Breast06 (n = 866) have confirmed the superior efficacy of trastuzumab deruxtecan vs capecitabine or a taxane, in terms of progression-free survival, in the treatment of patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-low or ultralow metastatic breast cancer [32]. The promising results for these drugs highlight the need for their incorporation into new treatment strategies for TNBC.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Our findings, including that of a strong association between pCR and long-term outcomes, should be considered in the context of the limitations of the JBCRG-22 study, which included the smaller-than-planned sample size and the time required to enroll the study participants. The current analyses are therefore not sufficiently powered to detect differences between treatment groups or the prognostic factor subgroups. Imbalances in patient characteristics, particularly age and histological grade, may have confounded some results. Owing to limitations in insurance-covered medical care, BRCA1/2 mutation status could not be determined for all enrolled patients with primary TNBC.

The pooling of data for patients treated with eribulin (groups A2, B1, and B2) in this exploratory study introduced heterogeneity in terms of partner drugs, treatment (including carboplatin for the patients in group A2 but not for those in groups B1 or B2), treatment duration, and patient characteristics (including HRD status between patients in group A2 and those in groups B1 and B2). Differences in discontinuation rates would also have influenced the results []. These factors need to be considered when interpreting the results, especiall33y those of the survival-outcome and biomarker analyses.

Although HRD status may have a significant influence on prognosis in cases of TNBC, multivariate analyses to identify prognostic factors were not feasible because of differences in treatment intensity between group A and group B. However, we analyzed the data for groups B1 + B2 separately, and the results showed generally the same trends as those found in groups A2 + B1 + B2 (data not shown).

Despite the limitations described above, the results may be useful to generate hypotheses that could be explored in larger, appropriately powered studies, including in the context of current treatment standards (platinum–taxane with or without immunotherapy).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: By providing hypothesis-generating signals regarding eribulin-based regimens, the results of this follow-up study investigating survival outcomes for patients enrolled in the JBCRG-22 study contribute to research into the potential role of eribulin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy in the treatment of selected TNBC patients (e.g., those with HRD-positive tumors or at higher risk of developing neuropathy), particularly when considering long-term prognosis. They suggest that stratification by HRD score is clinically important, as patients with HRD-positive tumors were more likely to achieve pCR and tended to have better survival than those with HRD-negative tumors. Additionally, our hypothesis-generating results regarding LC and NLR may be useful in the development of clinical prediction models for patients receiving eribulin-containing chemotherapy.
